content: I'm doing my thesis on evaluating Lean 4 proofs and need criteria to measure their quality. What standards or methodologies does the community use to determine if a proof is 'mathlib-grade' and ready to be merged into the GitHub repository?
What have you tried to find out yourself? For instance, have you considered searching zulip? What have you found?
(Or did you look at the leanprover-community webpage? There is also material there.)

How would this be measuring their quality , in any other sense than assigning it a vague “Mathlib” quality level , which is not some constant really.

Would you not want to have more well defined measures of quality if you plan to analyse code for a thesis ? The question should ultimately be how you’d define this “quality” as it would be a meta property since proofs are extensional , and we can’t easily reason about the internals of a proof. And I believe all information but their type is discarded after compilation so not like you can “run” different proofs to gauge their efficiency .

https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/ has the information for mathlib standards, in the left hand panel at the bottom is the section "contributing" which has the subsections like naming, comments, and code-style, etc...

I agree that mathlib isn’t an immutable, objective measure of 'quality.' However, as a community-trusted standard, it acts as a great empirical benchmark. Even if its inconsistent the general idea remains "if the largest library of formal proofs on lean accepts this proof it must be doing something right"... at least that's my thought process

Now for Lean proofs themselves

While yes of course proofs themselves are extensional; lean itself is still a programming language that still runs on hardware. Meaning, If a proof takes 15 minutes for the elaborator to process, that is a real computational bottleneck. From an optimization perspective, we can measure efficiency during the compilation/elaboration phase.

Another point is that defining anything interesting usually requires mathlib. But that reliance on mathlib means that proofs are vulnerable to constant updates. Proofs written in a "structured" or "clearer" way ensure that when mathlib inevitably changes, its simpler to find where and how the code was affected.

I’ve looked into this by consulting my professors and reading through mathlib source files. So far, I’ve picked up on a few core community standards, like the strict rules surrounding simp usage (keeping simp terminal and backed by clear lemmas) and the heavy emphasis on maximal generality to ensure definitions and proofs are as atomic and reusable as possible. I have not searched through zulip i'm still not really comfortable with using zulip yet...

Yousef Elbaz said:

Another point is that defining anything interesting usually requires mathlib.

In my view, the connection is a bit deeper than this. The most mainstream analogy I can think of is the relationship between the core R programming language and its tidyverse package ecosystem, and I think it is not a coincidence that both share common ancestry in Scheme. When a language provides a degree of extensibility via metaprogramming, I think it is almost inevitable that its popular libraries become highly coupled with usage of the language and that standards are more liable to travel both upstream and downstream of the core language.

Yousef Elbaz said:

While yes of course proofs themselves are extensional; lean itself is still a programming language that still runs on hardware. Meaning, If a proof takes 15 minutes for the elaborator to process, that is a real computational bottleneck. From an optimization perspective, we can measure efficiency during the compilation/elaboration phase.

This is not really true , you don’t have to rebuild most things for most purposes .

And it also is not as atomic as you seem to think, meaning a single proof elaborating slowly can be the result of more than just what is inside that proof, it is a complex relationship between your and the library’s overall design choices , and the ever changing nature of language / library itself.

Yes in Mathlib you measure and benchmark the build because it has to be rebuilt a lot and it’s used by everyone , but any single proof change speeds up and slows down other parts.

I don’t really know what you meant by the structured part , it seems like you were referring to readability , but this is in some tension with quality being about the elaboration.

TL; DR : I think you may be underestimating the difficulty in creating a well defined thesis concept of “ proof quality “ .
